summary: NASA Orbital Rescue is an interactive and educational web video game designed for children and youth, developed with the goal of bringing the history of space exploration and science closer in a dynamic and engaging way. Starting from the initial idea of simulating the rescue of forgotten space equipment in orbit, the player takes on the role of a commander piloting a NASA spacecraft through a vibrant space environment to locate historic artifacts and transmit their valuable scientific data back to Earth.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

NASA Orbital Rescue is an interactive, educational 2D space exploration web game designed for children and youth. The player takes on the role of a NASA rescue spacecraft commander on a mission to navigate an orbital map, locate, and recover 6 historic space artifacts: the Hubble Space Telescope, Voyager 1 Space Probe, Opportunity Rover, Apollo 11 Command Module, Explorer 1 Satellite, and Skylab Space Station.

  • Navigation and Radar: The spacecraft is piloted using smooth space physics (controlled thrust and inertia) alongside a radar system featuring on-screen proximity alerts and edge directional indicators to locate off-screen artifacts.
  • Rescue and Telemetry: Approaching each artifact triggers a visual and audio rescue sequence that opens a holographic data card displaying a vector illustration, mission year, key scientific contributions, and a fun fact. The player then presses a button to transmit the data back to Earth and earn science points.
  • Planetary Exploration: The environment features 6 interactive celestial bodies (Earth, The Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and Neptune). Clicking or tapping any planet opens a scientific fact sheet detailing NASA missions and their most important discoveries on that world.
  • Real-Time Translation: Using the 🌐 ES | EN toggle button, the entire interface, orbital labels, and educational cards switch instantly between Spanish and English without losing game progress.

2. What benefits does it offer?

  • Active, Playful Learning: Turns astronomical and historical facts into rewards within an interactive mission, improving comprehension and retention among students.
  • Scientific Bilingualism: Allows players to naturally practice technical and space-related vocabulary in both English and Spanish while playing.
  • Total Accessibility and Portability: Self-contained in a single lightweight .html file, requiring no installation, app stores, servers, or prior setup to run.
  • Cross-Platform Inclusion: Natively adapts its controls for both desktop computers (keyboard) and mobile phones or tablets (virtual touch joystick).

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Inspiring STEM Vocations: Sparking curiosity in astronomy, aerospace engineering, and science among elementary and middle-school students.
  • Teaching Tool for Educators: Serving as a free, easily shareable digital resource via email, messaging, or learning platforms to enrich science or language classes.
  • Accessible Science Outreach: Showcasing how past and current NASA missions have helped humanity better understand Earth and our Solar System.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Web Languages and Standards:
    • HTML5 (<canvas> and SVG): For real-time graphical rendering of the spacecraft, planets, parallax stars, particle effects, and scalable vector illustrations of each artifact.
    • CSS3 and Tailwind CSS: For responsive layout design, translucent holographic effects (backdrop-filter), and automatic adaptation to different screen sizes.
    • JavaScript (ES6+): For the orbital physics engine, collision detection, game state logic, touch/keyboard input handling, and the bilingual translation dictionary.
  • Native Browser APIs:
    • Web Audio API: Used to mathematically synthesize all sound effects (discoveries, planetary scans, data transmission, and victory fanfare) without relying on external audio files.
  • Software and Hardware:
    • Software: Modern web browsers (Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox) with responsive debugging tools and Google Fonts (Orbitron and Inter).
    • Hardware: Desktop/laptop computer for coding and keyboard testing, and touchscreen smartphones to validate virtual joystick ergonomics.

5. In what way is your project creative?

  • Integrated Holographic Encyclopedia: Rather than displaying static blocks of text, scientific information appears as "recovered transmissions" on a NASA-style onboard computer, weaving learning directly into the game's narrative.
  • Self-Contained Vector Art and Generative Audio: All illustrations were coded as scalable SVGs and sound effects are generated via real-time synthesized waveforms, delivering a rich audiovisual experience in a single portable file.
  • Dual-Layer Exploration: Combines a primary objective (rescuing the 6 spacecraft) with a secondary layer of free scientific curiosity (exploring the 6 host planets).

6. What factors did your team take into account?

  • Target Audience (Children and Youth): Used an encouraging tone ("Attention, Commander!"), vibrant high-contrast interfaces, and concise fun facts to sustain engagement.
  • Cross-Platform Ergonomics: Designed forgiving flight physics and an ergonomically placed virtual joystick for comfortable thumb control on mobile devices.
  • Educational Accuracy: Selected 6 real NASA missions spanning different eras (1958–2004) alongside verified planetary discoveries.
  • Ease of Distribution: Prioritized a single-file architecture so any teacher, parent, or student can launch the game with a single click on any device.
